units.text: You’ll learn where a global S three request goes, how to delegate one safely, and where to look for evidence. One global entry point doesn't mean the same file is present in every Region. Follow the client through the Multi-Region Access Point to an eligible bucket. Routing decides where the request goes; separately configured replication decides which copies are there.

A document might exist in the primary bucket but not yet in the alternate bucket. Before calling that path ready, check that the intended version exists and the access point, bucket, and encryption-key permissions let the application read it.

When you initiate a failover, the routing controls shift eligible traffic. Test an actual read and consider how any writes made in that Region will get back before switching back. A route change isn't a data recovery plan.

An inherited design may use S three Object Lambda to redact a returned object. The diagram explains that pattern, not a new-customer recommendation. Since November 2025, access has been limited to existing customers using it and selected partners. For a new design, evaluate supported processing alternatives.

Read the retention side as three different things. A vault lock belongs to the older Glacier vault API. S three Object Lock applies retention to eligible object versions. An S three Glacier storage class governs storage and retrieval; it isn't a prohibition on deleting a version.

How can a customer send a file without A W S credentials or routing it through your server? The app authorizes the request and signs a put for one object key and any required headers. The client sends the upload to S three directly over H T T P S.

The link comes with the signer's permissions and applicable policies. If the signing credentials expire first, so does access through the link. A request scoped to one operation is not a one-use link.

Use a distinct object key and verify the expected upload before making it visible. Treat the link as a bearer secret. Test expiry and incorrect requests rather than assuming the client will behave as expected.
A rise in access-denied errors tells you when something changed, but the chart won't tell you who made the call. Start with request metrics to narrow the time and scope.

To identify the caller and object action, correlate a matching CloudTrail data event. That evidence only exists when the selection covered the action. Management events aren't a substitute for object-level coverage.

Server access logs can supply details about requests but aren't a real-time feed. Compare the available records to the policies relevant to the request. A missing record is not evidence that the request never happened.

You’ll learn where an E B S volume can attach and how to choose its type and performance. Start with an E B S-backed instance that stops or is replaced. The E B S volume stores blocks separately from the instance, but the volume can attach only inside its Availability Zone. Moving compute to another zone doesn't move that volume with it.

Follow the middle arrow: create a snapshot, then create a new volume from it in the target zone. Attach the new volume to compute there. The snapshot is the recovery source; the first volume was never attached across zones.

The bottom example is a separate decision. Delete on termination controls whether an attached volume is removed when the instance terminates. Set and test that behavior for the particular volume rather than assuming persistence always saves it.

Start with how the workload reads and writes. Random, latency-sensitive work such as a boot disk or a transactional app fits SSD. General-purpose SSD is usually the starting comparison; use provisioned-I ops options when sustained I O and latency requirements justify them.

A large sequential scan is different. Throughput-oriented HDD can make sense for frequent sequential processing; cold HDD is aimed at less frequently accessed data. Both HDD families in the table are data volumes, not boot volumes.

On G P two, more capacity also raises baseline I ops. Smaller volumes can burst using credits, so a short benchmark may hide what happens under sustained load. Measure the workload after the burst window.

On G P three, choose capacity, I ops, and throughput separately within their limits. Think of a modest dataset that needs strong performance: you don't have to buy extra disk space simply to raise the performance setting.

You’ll learn to diagnose slow E B S storage and verify that a snapshot restore is usable. The workload says the disk is slow, but first follow the evidence. If the application asks for more I O than the path completes, requests accumulate in the queue and latency rises. Find the limiting layer before paying for a faster volume.

The path has three different limits: the app's I O size and queue depth, the E C two instance's E B S bandwidth, and the volume's own I ops and throughput. If the instance link is saturated, increasing only the volume setting won't clear the queue.

Follow data from the first snapshot to the second. E B S saves the blocks that changed after the previous snapshot, yet a restore from the second point can reconstruct the whole volume as it looked then. Incremental storage does not mean a partial restore.

A block-level snapshot doesn't know about an application's transactions. For a database, coordinate writes and use application-appropriate tooling when you need application consistency. Deleting an older snapshot doesn't remove blocks that another snapshot still requires.

To move into another Availability Zone in the same Region, create a new volume in the target zone from the regional snapshot. Attach it there and validate the data and application. You are restoring a new volume, not stretching the old one across zones.

An available volume can still have slower first reads while snapshot blocks initialize. If recovery time matters, plan how to initialize or evaluate an eligible Fast Snapshot Restore or provisioned initialization rate. Measure app readiness, not just volume creation.

You’ll learn to automate recovery points and make sure the recovery role can use the encryption key. Follow the loop: select supported tagged resources, schedule snapshot or A M I creation, then retain, expire, and optionally copy what the Data Lifecycle Manager policy creates. The policy doesn't manage every old snapshot just because it matches a tag.

Use Data Lifecycle Manager for an E C two and E B S lifecycle policy. Where you need one centralized backup plan across supported services, consider A W S Backup. Set retention from recovery requirements and verify it with a restore.

Encryption by default covers newly created E B S volumes and snapshot copies in the Region as applicable. It doesn't go back and encrypt the existing unencrypted volume. Plan a replacement from an encrypted snapshot rather than assuming a switch rewrites old data.

The drawing is a same-account, same-Region restore. The recovery role needs to use the customer-managed key; otherwise the restore path can stop at the key check. After creating and attaching the volume, verify the mount, data and application. Permission alone doesn't prove recovery.

You’ll learn when E B S Multi-Attach fits and what still has to coordinate the writers. Multi-Attach presents one shared I O one or I O two block volume to supported E C two instances in the same Availability Zone. A cluster-aware application or file system must coordinate the writers. Otherwise, simultaneous updates can collide on disk.

This is not a shared NFS or SMB directory and not a cross-zone design. When the requirement is a normal shared file service, choose a file service instead. When the requirement is coordinated shared blocks, validate workload and instance support first.
